content: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) has outlined a global agenda for sustainable development by 2030, emphasizing the importance of inclusive health systems and services for all individuals, including those with disabilities. 2. WHO has been actively involved in promoting assistive devices and technologies to improve the quality of life for individuals with disabilities, as detailed in their global disability action plan for 2014–2021. This plan aims to enhance health outcomes for people with disabilities through better access to rehabilitation and assistive services. 3. The WHO's Rehabilitation 2030 initiative calls for action to strengthen rehabilitation services worldwide, ensuring they are accessible, integrated, and sustainable. 4. The Global Cooperation on Assistive Technology (GATE) program by WHO focuses on increasing access to affordable and high-quality assistive products, particularly in low-resource settings. 5. Research and guidelines emphasize the critical role of prosthetics and orthotics in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), highlighting their impact on health, mobility, and social inclusion. 6. Community-based rehabilitation (CBR) guidelines developed by WHO provide a framework for integrating rehabilitation services into community health systems, ensuring accessibility for individuals in underserved areas. 7. The WHO has also developed standards for prosthetics and orthotics services, emphasizing the need for competent professionals, appropriate training, and adherence to technical and safety standards. 8. The importance of interdisciplinary teamwork in chronic care, including rehabilitation, has been highlighted in systematic reviews, demonstrating improved outcomes when healthcare teams collaborate effectively. 9. Guidelines for the management of specific conditions, such as diabetic foot ulcers and stroke rehabilitation, underscore the need for evidence-based practices and user-centered approaches in prosthetics and orthotics services. 10. 11. Workforce planning and training in prosthetics and orthotics are essential to meet national and global demands. This includes aligning training programs with international standards and ensuring continuing professional development for practitioners. 12. Governments are encouraged to take a leading role in developing and coordinating national policies for prosthetics and orthotics services, involving all relevant stakeholders, including service users and caregivers. 13. Data collection and monitoring of prosthetics and orthotics services at national and regional levels are crucial for identifying unmet needs and improving service delivery. 14. 15. Strategies to raise awareness about the benefits of prosthetics and orthotics services should be implemented, emphasizing their role in improving health, mobility, and social participation. 16. The provision of prosthetics and orthotics services should be inclusive, accessible to all individuals in need, and integrated into the broader healthcare system. 17. 18. User-centered service delivery models should involve service users and their representatives in decision-making processes, from policy development to service evaluation. 19. Training programs for prosthetics and orthotics professionals should be available at various levels to address national needs, with a focus on competency and adherence to best practices. 20. Governments and stakeholders should collaborate internationally to share research, data, and experiences in prosthetics and orthotics service provision, fostering innovation and improvement.
